skills/build-rbac/SKILL.md:
---
name: build-rbac
description: Design, build, extend, troubleshoot, or security-review role-based access control (RBAC), including users, roles, permissions, tenant memberships, API authorization, admin UI, and authorization tests. Use for RBAC system creation or integration in existing projects.
---

# RBAC Builder

Act as an implementation partner. Match the user's language; use English identifiers in code. This plugin supplies engineering instructions, not a running identity service or database. Never imply it has connected tools or deployed an application when it has not.

## Owner requirements

This owner builds English listening/learning apps and hotel/entertainment-center management systems. Aim for a reusable, extensible foundation with student/customer/teacher/staff roles and overlapping domain profiles, tenant/branch scope, authentication lifecycle, backend/frontend daily technical logs, durable database login history and user-action audit. Use references/application-foundation.md whenever designing or implementing these concerns. Redis is a configurable adapter for shared state and acceleration; never use it as the sole authoritative permission or audit store. Deliver requirements and implementation in stages without dropping these concerns or claiming a skills-only plugin is a deployed system.

The owner also requires multilingual React interfaces and multiple switchable themes. Use references/frontend-design.md for every frontend implementation: default zh-CN/en locales, extensible locale namespaces, reusable accessible design tokens, separate named theme palettes and light/dark/system modes, user preference persistence and localization/theme acceptance checks. Preserve existing UI conventions and distinguish student/customer experiences from staff administration.

## Discover and decide

For an existing repository, inspect AGENTS.md, architecture, authentication, schema, endpoints, UI, migrations and tests before editing. Respect the existing framework and identity provider. Ask only questions that materially change implementation: new or existing project; stack; single or multiple tenants; resource ownership/data scopes; identity provider. Continue independent work while awaiting optional answers. When starting from scratch without stack requirements, use the owner's preferred stack: FastAPI + SQLAlchemy + Alembic + Pydantic + React and use SQLite for a local prototype, PostgreSQL for production planning. State assumptions. Do not create a hosted website unless requested. Follow the host's applicable artifact/storage and deployment rules.

Use references/security-design.md for design and review; references/acceptance.md for test coverage. Consult official framework documentation for version-sensitive API details, and use installed versions and lockfiles. Never invent citations, dependencies or execution results.

## Deliver a concrete design

Define users, roles, immutable permission codes such as `invoice.read`, role-permission and user-role relationships, and optional tenant memberships. Reuse existing authorization facilities when they meet requirements; otherwise model roles and permissions explicitly. Establish a permission matrix with actor, action, resource, scope and allow/deny outcomes. Treat menus/routes as presentation, not the authoritative permission catalog.

Separate authentication from authorization. Use a central authorization service invoked on every protected backend operation. Default deny, least privilege, and scope all queries before retrieving objects. Explain how permissions and object scope combine. Tenant-scoped roles must not leak into other tenants. Avoid role-name checks scattered throughout business code. Do not add complex inheritance or explicit denies unless needed; if used, define precedence, detect cycles, and test conflicts. Distinguish platform administration from tenant administration.

## Implement end to end

Work in the repository when available; otherwise create the complete requested project artifact using supported host workflows. Implement schema and constraints, migrations, permission catalog, idempotent bootstrap, authorization services, protected APIs, administration UI when requested, and tests. Integrate the existing authentication system; do not roll custom cryptography or store plaintext passwords. Use framework session/CSRF controls or established OIDC/JWT validation. Never trust role, permission or tenant claims supplied by the client without server validation.

For FastAPI, implement reusable authentication and permission dependencies with Depends/Security and a central authorization service. OAuth2 scopes describe capabilities but do not replace database role grants or object/tenant checks. Use SQLAlchemy models and Alembic migrations, Pydantic request/response schemas, tenant-scoped queries and server-side ownership validation. Cover list/create/detail/custom/bulk operations separately. Use one request-scoped database session and explicit transaction ownership; do not mix synchronous blocking database calls into async routes without a deliberate strategy. Validate JWT signature, allowed algorithm, issuer, audience and expiry with an established library; make revocation semantics explicit. Keep role/tenant/permission assignment fields out of ordinary profile update schemas. Test dependencies and HTTP endpoints with pytest and a compatible FastAPI/HTTPX client, using isolated databases and representative identities.

For React, provide current-user permissions, a permission-aware component/hook, protected navigation, accessible permission-management forms and clear error/loading states. Keep every decision enforced on the server. Avoid exposing secrets in bundles or localStorage. Follow the project's authentication storage conventions, favoring secure cookies when appropriate.

Protect assignment and revocation operations. Require an administrative permission and restrict grants to the administrator's delegated authority and tenant. Prevent self-escalation and unintended removal of the last recoverable administrator. Log sensitive changes with actor, target, tenant, action, timestamp and outcome without credentials or tokens. Define transaction boundaries, revocation behavior, session/token invalidation and permission-cache invalidation.

## Verify and hand off

Run relevant tests, migrations and build/type checks as available. Include allowed and forbidden cases and object/tenant boundaries. Describe checks actually run and any blocked checks. Report changed files, usage, bootstrap instructions and remaining assumptions. Never claim deployment or production readiness without evidence. Use existing development conventions and environment variables; never hardcode production secrets. Obtain approval only when required for actions outside authorized scope, such as destructive production data changes or external publication.

Personal appearance is an explicit owner requirement: every user can save their own language and theme. Include visual-comfort palette options and optional calm background materials according to references/frontend-design.md, while preserving readable contrast and avoiding medical protection claims. Distinguish interface language from learning-content language.
# Authorization acceptance cases

Construct tests from the permission matrix, not merely from implementation branches.

| Case | Expected result |
| --- | --- |
| Anonymous or inactive actor on protected operation | Denied |
| Assigned active role with required permission and scope | Allowed |
| Missing permission or unknown action | Denied |
| User changes object ID to another owner's object | Denied unless policy explicitly grants access |
| User changes tenant ID or calls another tenant's endpoint | Denied with no data disclosure |
| List/search/export/count/nested resources | Only authorized scope returned |
| Create/update supplies role, owner or tenant outside authority | Rejected or safely server-assigned |
| Unprivileged direct API call despite hidden UI control | Denied |
| Tenant administrator attempts platform role or broader grant | Denied |
| Permission revoked while sessions/cache are active | Meets documented revocation policy |
| Role removal, duplicate grant, concurrent grant/revoke | Consistent transactional state |
| Sensitive role/permission change | Audit event exists without secrets |

Also test each custom endpoint and bulk operation; asynchronous jobs must revalidate authority or follow an explicitly documented execution-time policy. For existing applications add regression cases proving a real boundary, not shallow tests that reproduce implementation logic.

## Extension and operational acceptance

Test student own/enrolled versus another student's progress; customer own versus another customer's booking; staff assigned branch versus another branch; overlapping student/customer identities and role revocation; module registration without unintended grants. Exercise Redis unavailable/restarted/evicted/stale keys, cross-worker invalidation and documented revocation bounds. Verify audit transaction rollback and outbox retries/deduplication, denied attempt persistence, append-only access and export authorization. Verify login failure without user ID, session revocation, sensitive data redaction, malicious frontend telemetry, log injection/path traversal, daily rotation/retention and multi-worker log handling. Audit history must survive cache deletion and ordinary users must not alter it.

## Frontend acceptance

Use references/frontend-design.md to validate multilingual core flows and error/accessibility text, long translations, locale/timezone formatting, language persistence, named themes and light/dark/system modes, user/tenant preference precedence, responsive layouts and component/portal/chart token coverage. UI permission visibility never replaces backend enforcement.

# Extensible application foundation

## Boundaries and domain roles
Build a modular monolith first unless scale or organizational requirements justify services. Separate identity/authentication, authorization, organizations/tenants, domain profiles, observability and audit. Expose stable interfaces for authorization, events and storage. Do not claim RBAC alone supplies a complete application foundation.

A User is an identity; Membership connects it to a tenant; RoleAssignment grants authority within tenant and optionally organization/branch scopes. Student, customer, teacher and employee profiles carry domain data and can overlap for one identity. Profile existence alone must not confer permission. Anonymous visitors, registered customers and paying subscribers are distinct states. Entitlements (subscription, course enrollment, booking access) are distinct from staff authority.

Use immutable namespaced permissions such as learning.lesson.read, learning.progress.read_own, hotel.booking.manage and venue.reservation.check_in. Model scopes explicitly (own/enrolled/assigned/branch/tenant/platform); don't infer them solely from names. Learning progress requires ownership or authorized teaching relationship; bookings require customer ownership or authorized staff branch access. Define role templates per module, idempotent registration and migrations. Adding a module must not silently broaden existing roles. Avoid free-form arbitrary SQL policy expressions.

Optional hierarchy: organization, branch/property/venue, team. Clarify which scopes actually apply. Plan versioned APIs, shared SDK/types, pagination, filtering, indexes, migration compatibility and extension contracts. Prefer a modular monolith over prematurely deploying microservices.

## Redis adapter
Offer configurable Redis support, not an unconditional dependency for small single-process prototypes. Production multi-worker deployments often benefit from shared sessions, atomic rate limiting, permission cache and revocation coordination. PostgreSQL is authoritative for roles, assignments, login history and audit history.

Namespace keys by environment, application, tenant and subject; include authorization version and bound TTLs. Increment permission versions transactionally with grants/revokes and reconcile caches reliably. Do not rely solely on Redis Pub/Sub for durable invalidation. Describe the exact maximum revocation delay; TTL alone is eventual revocation. Recheck sensitive writes against authoritative state.

Separate evictable caches from security-critical session/revocation state and queues (logical Redis DB numbers do not isolate memory eviction policy). Define persistence, capacity, timeout and outage behavior per use. Database-backed permission checks may be a safe cache fallback; session or revocation failures must not bypass authentication. Shared rate limits must not silently become per-worker limits. A durable outbox and retryable idempotent consumers are required when asynchronous audit delivery must survive failures.

## Technical logs
Emit structured backend JSON logs with UTC timestamp, severity, service, environment, release, request/trace ID, route template, status, duration, tenant/user identifiers where justified and sanitized exception metadata. Generate trustworthy correlation IDs server-side; validate supplied IDs. Do not record request bodies, auth headers, cookies, passwords, tokens or personal booking/student data by default.

Frontend telemetry covers uncaught errors, rejected promises and selected API failures; scrub URLs/query strings and form values. Frontend reports are untrusted telemetry, not proof of a user action. Send bounded batches to an authenticated or tightly limited ingestion endpoint with size/schema/rate controls and sampled duplicate suppression. Correlate to server-issued request IDs and releases. No remote script execution or arbitrary file access.

For file-managed deployments provide daily rotation with retention, compression and disk caps, UTC rotation by default and configurable display timezone (Asia/Shanghai for this owner). Do not have multiple workers rotate/write a shared file using an unsafe handler: use a collector/queue listener or per-worker files. For containers prefer stdout/stderr plus external collection and daily archival. Never promise browser-side server log files without an ingestion service.

Log-management UI/API supports authorized date/severity/service/correlation searches, pagination and audited export. Use allowlisted logical log identifiers, not client-provided filesystem paths; prevent traversal and symlink escapes. Avoid exposing stack traces/secrets to ordinary users. Define retention, access control, backup and recovery policies per data type; ask about operational requirements rather than inventing legal retention periods.

## Login and security history
Store durable auth events separately from current sessions: login success/failure, logout, refresh failures, lockout, password reset, MFA changes, forced revocation. Capture event ID, timestamp, actor ID when known, tenant/app context, outcome, normalized reason code, minimally necessary IP/user-agent/device metadata and correlation ID. Failed login may have no known user; avoid storing raw attempted identities unnecessarily. Never store plaintext session/refresh tokens. Use bounded queries and indexes on tenant, user and timestamp. Derive client IP only from trusted proxy configuration.

Implement refresh rotation/reuse detection when refresh tokens are used, session/device listing and authorized force logout. Password recovery and MFA follow the identity provider/framework; don't invent crypto.

## User action audit
Server-side business services create durable audit records for meaningful operations: role grants/revokes, profile updates, learning completion, booking changes, cancellations, check-in and authorized exports. Record actor, optional impersonator, tenant/scope, namespaced action, target type/ID, outcome, timestamp, correlation/event ID and allowlisted redacted changes. Keep business audit separate from high-volume page-view analytics.

For committed writes, use the same database transaction or transactional outbox so state and audit agree. Define retry/idempotency and ordering. Denied/failed attempts need a separate durable security event path because the business transaction may roll back. Define policy for audit storage failure, especially privileged writes.

Application accounts have insert-only audit access where practical; log readers are separately authorized. Do not expose ordinary edit/delete endpoints for audit events. Append-only permissions reduce tampering but are not absolute tamper proof; use external immutable archival/signing only when required. Retention deletion is a controlled, documented administrative process. Audit access/export must itself be auditable.

## Operational deliverables
Produce module boundaries, schema/ERD, scope-aware permission matrix, API contract, Redis/cache/revocation strategy, log/audit event schemas, retention configuration, administrator bootstrap, backup/restore and upgrade guide. Supply local environment examples without secrets and optional PostgreSQL/Redis compose services when requested. Implement incrementally: core identity/RBAC, domain integration, logging/audit, Redis and operations. Do not call the package production ready without implementation, deployment verification and meaningful boundary tests.

References to verify for current implementation:
- https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/
- https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/
- https://alembic.sqlalchemy.org/
- https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/
- https://redis.io/docs/latest/management/persistence/
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html

# Frontend design, internationalization and themes

## Default direction
The owner explicitly requires multilingual interfaces and multiple switchable themes. Default new React projects to TypeScript with a clean, contemporary admin design: clear typography, consistent spacing, restrained color, responsive navigation, accessible forms and dense but readable tables. Keep this a configurable baseline, not a mandatory visual brand. Preserve an existing component library and conventions. For new projects choose a maintained accessible component system after checking current documentation; do not introduce competing UI frameworks. Customer/student interfaces should be simpler and task-oriented; staff administration may be denser. Share tokens/components without imposing the same navigation on every persona.

Define reusable layout, navigation, breadcrumbs, table/filter/pagination, modal, form validation, notifications, empty/loading/error/forbidden states and settings screens. Cover user/role/permission management, scoped role grants, session/login history, audit search/export and technical-log access. Destructive or privileged operations need clear contextual feedback. Menus and buttons reflect permissions; server authorization remains mandatory.

## Internationalization
Use a centralized i18n provider and namespaced locale dictionaries, with stable semantic message keys rather than Chinese/English source text as identifiers. Default locales zh-CN and en; allow future languages without rewriting components. Use an established library such as react-i18next when compatible with the repository, verifying version-sensitive setup against official docs. Avoid hardcoded visible text, including validation, modal text, toasts, table headers, accessibility labels, empty states and loading/error messages.

Backend returns stable machine error codes plus parameters; frontend maps them to localized messages with a safe fallback. Never localize permission codes, API keys or database identifiers. Role/permission/module display names may be localized with fallback; custom user-defined names remain data rather than translation keys. Support pluralization and interpolation; do not concatenate translated sentence fragments or render untrusted translation HTML.

Format date/time, numbers and currency with Intl using locale plus explicit user timezone/currency settings. Store timestamps in UTC and display the configured timezone. Language, timezone and currency are distinct preferences. Prepare layout for long labels, text expansion and future RTL through logical CSS properties and document lang/dir. Do not claim RTL support is complete until visually tested.

Provide an accessible language switcher. Resolve language in documented order: explicit authenticated user preference, remembered anonymous preference, supported browser locale, application default. Persist user preferences through a profile/settings API; use local storage only for nonsensitive anonymous display preferences. Reconcile anonymous settings at login deliberately rather than silently overriding the account.

## Theme architecture
Separate theme palette from display mode. Support light, dark and system modes by default, plus extensible named palettes/brands (for example neutral, blue or green) through semantic CSS variables/design tokens. A palette must define both light and dark values if supported. Do not market three display modes as three independently designed themes. New named palettes can be configured without rewriting components.

Tokenize background/surface/text/muted/border/primary/danger/success/focus, spacing, typography, radii, shadows and chart colors. Apply tokens consistently to dialogs, tooltips, portals, tables, charts and icons; avoid scattered hardcoded colors. Follow system changes only in system mode. Initialize theme before first paint where the runtime supports it to avoid flash and hydration mismatch. Respect reduced motion and visible focus. Validate contrast, keyboard navigation and non-color status indicators across supported palettes/modes.

Offer separate theme and mode controls with preview and reset. Persist preferences per user and optionally tenant brand defaults; user mode/language preferences must not be overwritten by tenant branding. Document precedence: explicit user setting, remembered anonymous setting, tenant/app default; system mode then resolves using OS preference. Validate theme identifiers against an allowlist; never accept arbitrary CSS/JS from customers. Include theme schema version/fallback for deleted themes.

## Acceptance and handoff
Verify language switching across all core screens, missing-key fallback, translated backend errors, pluralization, long text, accessible names, date/time/currency formatting, and login/logout preference reconciliation. Verify named palette switching and light/dark/system behavior, OS changes, persistence across reloads/devices for account settings, token coverage including portals/charts, and no unauthorized UI/API access after role changes.

Use focused component/E2E tests and visual inspection at representative desktop/mobile sizes. Report actual checks and incomplete RTL/browser coverage. Deliver design tokens, locale namespaces, preference API schema, reusable components and a concise extension guide for adding a language or theme. Add frontend requirements to the project acceptance matrix rather than leaving them as optional decoration.

Official implementation references to consult for current versions:
- https://www.i18next.com/
- https://react.i18next.com/
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl
- https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/

## Personal appearance settings and visual comfort
Each user can independently set interface language, named theme palette, light/dark/system mode, text size and reduced-motion preference through an accessible personal-settings screen with live preview, save and reset. Persist authenticated settings in the database through a validated self-service API; users must not modify another user's preferences. Apply across devices after login. Document handling of local anonymous preferences and account settings. Display-language changes do not automatically translate user content or switch learning-content language.

Include complete token sets for these starter palettes, each with an explicitly tested supported display mode:
- Soft neutral: off-white canvas, soft gray surfaces and clearly contrasting charcoal text.
- Warm reading: warm ivory/beige surfaces and dark brown/charcoal text; good for reading-focused layouts.
- Calm sage: muted green accents and neutral reading surfaces.
- Low-glare dark: dark charcoal surfaces, readable soft light text and restrained accents; avoid large bright white areas.

Describe these as visual-comfort options, not medical eye protection or proof that blue-light reduction prevents injury. Do not assume dark mode is comfortable for everyone. Preserve adequate text/control contrast and focus indicators; low-glare backgrounds must not become low-contrast text.

Optional theme materials include subtle botanical, paper-like or soft-gradient backgrounds, restrained monochrome icons and non-distracting empty-state illustrations. Make decorative materials opt-in and removable, with a plain-background setting. Keep textures/images outside primary reading areas, forms and dense tables; no animated/flashing scenery. Use configurable opacity, lightweight assets and solid-color fallbacks. Avoid background images conveying essential meaning; mark purely decorative imagery accordingly. Verify contrast over the actual rendered asset, not only base tokens.

Use existing code-native SVG/CSS assets where appropriate, or the image-generation skill for requested raster creation; do not claim theme assets have been generated when only specifying them. Include asset licensing/provenance, contained paths and extension guidance with the implementation. Evaluate all supplied palettes at representative desktop/mobile sizes with long translations and enlarged text.

# Design and review checklist

- Model User, Role, Permission, RolePermission and UserRole explicitly or map them to native framework facilities. Add Tenant and Membership for multi-tenancy. Tenant roles and assignments require tenant-aware uniqueness and referential integrity.
- Define each permission by resource/action; ownership, team and tenant scope are additional authorization conditions. A role grants capabilities, not ownership of all objects.
- Derive tenant context from authenticated membership, validating any requested tenant against it. Scope detail, list, search, export, counts, aggregates, files and background jobs alike. Do not leak inaccessible data through serializers, nested relations or errors.
- Deny anonymous, inactive and unauthorized actors. Choose consistent 401/403/404 behavior according to framework and information-disclosure policy.
- Evaluate authorization on writes and administrative operations inside appropriate transaction boundaries. Validate protected fields on create/update; prohibit mass assignment of role, owner and tenant fields.
- Define revocation consistency. Short-lived signed tokens may retain claims until expiry; use server-side permission lookup, token/session version checks or equivalent controls when immediate revocation is required. Invalidate caches across workers and tenants.
- Administrative grants must stay within delegated scope. Make permission catalogs server-owned and role changes auditable. Bootstrap administrators through a secure, documented path without default passwords.
- RBAC is insufficient for some contextual policies; describe added attribute/relationship checks explicitly rather than falsely claiming RBAC solves every access rule.
- Only add MFA, approval flows, separation of duties, role inheritance or external policy engines where requirements justify them.
